questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Plane through three intercepts
questions.learningObjective: write the intercept form of a plane from three axis cuts
questions.stem: Sheet 4101 asks the cartographer to write the equation of the flat patch that meets the three coordinate axes at 3, 4 and 5 units.

options.text: The equation x divided by 3 plus y divided by 4 plus z divided by 5 equals 1
The equation 3x plus 4y plus 5z equals 1, using the intercepts as coefficients
options.misconception: uses the intercepts as coefficients, not denominators

options.text: The equation x plus y plus z equals 12, the sum of the three intercepts
options.misconception: adds the intercept values into a single constant

options.text: The equation 5x plus 4y plus 3z equals 60, the product of the intercepts
options.misconception: builds an equation from the product of the intercepts

questions.explanation: A plane cutting the axes at a, b and c has the intercept form x over a plus y over b plus z over c equals 1. Using the intercepts as coefficients describes a different plane.
questions.hint: Each intercept goes in the denominator of its own term.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: state what makes two planes parallel
questions.stem: Sheet 4102 notes two level surfaces of a terraced landscape and asks what makes two planes parallel.

options.text: They have the same distance from the origin, whatever their normals

options.text: Their normal vectors point in the same direction, possibly with different lengths
They contain the same two intercepts on the coordinate axes
options.misconception: believes shared intercepts define parallel planes

options.text: They are described by equations whose left-hand coefficients are identical
options.misconception: requires identical coefficients instead of proportional ones

questions.explanation: Two planes are parallel exactly when their normal vectors are parallel. Identical coefficients describe only the special case where the normals happen to match exactly.
questions.hint: Compare the direction of the normals.

questions.explanation: The distance is the absolute value of the plane expression, 14, divided by the length of the normal, 5, giving 2.8. Using 14 without the division would report an unnormalised quantity.

options.misconception: confuses an intersection of planes with a tangency point

options.text: A straight line, since two nonparallel planes cut each other in a line

questions.stem: Sheet 4133 describes a surface cutting the axes at 3, 6 and 3 units and asks for the coefficient of y once the denominators are cleared.
questions.explanation: Clearing the denominators gives 2x plus y plus 2z equals 6, so the coefficient of y is 1. The intercepts are 3, 6 and 3.
questions.hint: Clear the denominators of the intercept form.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Unit tangent vector to a space curve
questions.learningObjective: explain why a tangent vector is normalised
questions.stem: Sheet 4134 asks why the tangent vector of a space curve must be normalised before it is used as a direction.

options.text: Because the derivative of a position vector always has unit length
options.misconception: assumes the derivative is already normalised

options.text: Because a unit tangent lets the curve be measured with arc length
options.misconception: gives a true but unrelated reason, not the length reason

options.text: Because the derivative carries the speed, which changes how fast the curve is followed
Because two curves can share a tangent only when it is a unit vector
options.misconception: invents a rule about shared tangents

questions.explanation: The derivative of the position vector has the length of the speed along the curve. A tangent already in use as a direction must have length one.
questions.hint: The derivative carries the speed, not the direction alone.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Distance from a point to a plane
questions.learningObjective: identify the segment that measures a plane distance
questions.stem: Sheet 4135 asks which line segment gives the distance from a point to a plane.

options.text: The segment from the point straight down to the horizontal plane below it
options.misconception: measures the vertical drop rather than the normal distance

options.text: The segment from the point to the closest point on the z axis
options.misconception: measures the distance to an axis rather than to the plane

options.text: The segment from the origin to the point where the plane meets that axis
options.misconception: measures a distance from the origin, not from the point

options.text: The segment from the point along the normal direction to the plane

questions.explanation: The distance to a plane is measured along the perpendicular to that plane, which is the direction of its normal. A vertical drop is correct only when the plane happens to be horizontal.
questions.hint: Measure along the normal direction.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Distance between parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: compute the separation of parallel planes
questions.stem: Sheet 4136 asks for the distance between the parallel planes x plus 2y equals 5 and 2x plus 4y equals 14.
questions.explanation: The second plane divides by 2 into x plus 2y equals 7, so the constants differ by 2 and the normal has length the root of 5, giving 0.8944.
questions.hint: Rewrite both planes with the same normal.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line as the intersection of two planes
questions.learningObjective: describe the line where two planes meet
questions.stem: Sheet 4137 asks for the equation of the line where the planes x plus y plus z equals 6 and x minus y equals 2 meet.

options.text: The line has y free, with x equal to 2 plus y and z equal to 4 minus 2y
The line has only the single point where y equals 1
options.misconception: reduces a line of solutions to one point

options.text: The line requires y to equal 1, since the two equations differ by 2y
options.misconception: reads a single coordinate value as the whole solution set

options.text: The line has x free, with y equal to x minus 2 and z equal to 8 minus 2x
options.misconception: solves for the wrong free variable and a different line

questions.explanation: Solving the two equations together leaves one free parameter, here y, and the other two coordinates follow from it. A single point would be the answer only if a third equation were added.
questions.hint: Subtract the equations, then let one coordinate vary.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Unit vectors along a direction
questions.learningObjective: correct a flawed normalisation of a direction
questions.stem: Sheet 4138 reports that a direction vector was normalised by dividing every component by the sum of the components, and asks for the correction.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since any common factor keeps the direction the same
options.misconception: overlooks that the factor must be the length

options.text: Divide by the length of the vector, which is the square root of the sum of squares
Divide by the largest component, since that is the dominant direction
options.misconception: normalises by the biggest component instead of the length

options.text: Divide by the square of the length, since the direction is a squared quantity
options.misconception: invents a squared normalisation rule

questions.explanation: A unit vector is the original vector divided by its length, the square root of the sum of the squared components. Dividing by the sum of the components changes the direction.
questions.hint: Divide each component by the vector's length.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Magnitude of a vector in space
questions.learningObjective: compute the length of a vector in space
questions.stem: Sheet 4139 asks for the length of the survey vector with components 2, 3 and 6 units.
questions.explanation: The length is the square root of 4 plus 9 plus 36, which is 7. The components are perpendicular, so they are combined that way.
questions.hint: Square each component, add them, take the root.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: read parallelism from a labelled diagram
questions.stem: Sheet 4140 draws two flat terraces with the same tilt, and asks what must be true of their labels.

options.text: Their constants on the right must be equal, since they share a tilt
options.misconception: confuses a shared tilt with a shared position

options.text: Their normal vectors must have different lengths, since they are separate
options.misconception: credits a length difference to the separation of the planes

options.text: Their normals must point the same way, while the constants may differ
Their constants must differ by exactly one, since they are adjacent
options.misconception: invents a unit spacing rule for parallel planes

questions.explanation: The tilt of a plane comes from its normal, so parallel terraces share a normal direction. A unit difference between the constants is not required.
questions.hint: The normal carries the tilt, the constant the height.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Magnitude of a vector in space
questions.learningObjective: check a computed vector length
questions.stem: Sheet 4141 reports a length computed from a vector with components 6, 8 and 0, and asks for the check.

options.text: The length 14 is right, since the components should be added
options.misconception: adds the components instead of rooting the sum of squares

options.text: The length 10 is right, but it should have been rounded to a whole number
options.misconception: invents a rounding requirement for a length

options.text: The length 10 is right, so the survey needs no further check
options.misconception: accepts a value without checking which rule produced it

options.text: The length 10 is right, since the root of 36 plus 64 plus 0 is 10

questions.explanation: The length is the square root of the sum of the squared components, and 36 plus 64 gives exactly 10. Adding the components would give 14, which overstates the straight-line distance.
questions.hint: Square each component, add them, then take the root.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: read a component of a parallel normal
questions.stem: Sheet 4142 gives two parallel surfaces with normals (1,2,3) and (2,4,6) and asks for the third component of the second normal.
questions.explanation: The second normal (2,4,6) is twice the first (1,2,3), so its third component is 6. Proportional normals are the test for parallel planes.
questions.hint: Compare the two normal vectors component by component.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line as the intersection of two planes
questions.learningObjective: state the direction of an intersection line
questions.stem: Sheet 4143 asks what a surveyor can say about the direction of the line where two planes meet.

options.text: Its direction is perpendicular to both normal vectors of the planes
Its direction is parallel to both normal vectors of the planes
options.misconception: makes the line parallel to the normals that define it

options.text: Its direction is the sum of the two normal vectors
options.misconception: builds the direction by adding the normals

options.text: Its direction is perpendicular to the line joining the two origins
options.misconception: invents a direction from a point that may not be relevant

questions.explanation: The direction of the intersection line is perpendicular to each plane, hence perpendicular to both normals. Adding them would not give a direction lying in both planes.
questions.hint: The direction is perpendicular to both normals.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Distance between parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: compare the gap between planes and between lines
questions.stem: Sheet 4144 asks a cartographer to compare the gap between two parallel planes with the gap between two parallel lines.

options.text: They are the same, because both are measured to the nearest point
options.misconception: ignores that line and plane gaps use different normals

options.text: Both use the constant difference divided by the normal length, in the same form
The plane gap is always larger, since a plane has more dimensions
options.misconception: claims a dimension count changes the formula

options.text: The line gap is always larger, since lines have no orientation to normalise
options.misconception: invents an orientation argument for the line case

questions.explanation: The same rule works in both settings: take the difference of the constants and divide by the length of the normal. In the plane case the normal has three components.
questions.hint: The same constant difference over the normal length.

questions.topic: Line as the intersection of two planes
questions.learningObjective: solve a pair of plane equations for a point
questions.stem: Sheet 4145 asks for the x coordinate of the point on the line where x plus y plus z equals 6 and x minus y equals 2, taken where y equals 0.
questions.explanation: The second equation gives x equal to 2 plus y, and the first then gives z equal to 4 minus 2y, so with y equal to 0 the point has x equal to 2.
questions.hint: Solve the pair of equations for one free coordinate.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Plane through three intercepts
questions.learningObjective: explain the convenience of the intercept form
questions.stem: Sheet 4146 asks why the intercept form of a plane is convenient on a survey sheet.

options.text: Because it avoids fractions when all three intercepts are equal
options.misconception: gives a special case instead of the general reason

options.text: Because it makes the normal vector of the plane obvious
options.misconception: claims the intercept form reveals the normal directly

options.text: Because the cut distances on the three axes appear directly in the equation
Because it works only for planes that meet the axes at equal distances
options.misconception: restricts the form to a special family of planes

questions.explanation: The intercept form puts the three cut distances straight into the equation, one per variable, which is easy to read on a survey sheet. It says nothing about the normal.
questions.hint: The cut distances appear directly in the equation.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Distance from a point to a plane
questions.learningObjective: check whether a point lies in a plane
questions.stem: Sheet 4147 reports that a point was declared to lie in a plane because the plane expression at that point came out as zero, and asks for the check.

options.text: The test is wrong, because the point must instead be compared with the normal
options.misconception: proposes a comparison that cannot decide membership

options.text: The test is wrong, because only points on the axes satisfy a plane equation
options.misconception: restricts the plane equation to the axes

options.text: The test is wrong, because the expression must be divided by the normal length first
options.misconception: confuses a membership test with a distance calculation

options.text: The test is right, since the plane expression vanishes exactly on the plane

questions.explanation: A point lies in a plane exactly when substituting it into the plane equation gives zero, so the test is sound. Dividing by the normal length would turn the check into a distance.
questions.hint: The plane expression vanishes exactly on the plane.

questions.topic: Unit vectors along a direction
questions.learningObjective: compute a component of a unit direction
questions.stem: Sheet 4148 asks for the first component of the unit vector along the survey direction 5, 0, 12.
questions.explanation: The direction vector has length 13, so the first component of the unit vector is 5 over 13, which is about 0.3846, and the other entries follow the same rule.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Unit tangent vector to a space curve
questions.learningObjective: predict the unit tangent when a curve is reversed
questions.stem: Sheet 4149 asks what happens to the unit tangent when a curve is traversed in the opposite direction.

options.text: It reverses sign, since the derivative also reverses
It stays the same, since the curve itself has not changed
options.misconception: ignores that the direction of travel has changed

options.text: It becomes zero, since the speed is the same in both directions
options.misconception: claims a zero result from reversing a direction

options.text: It is unchanged in length but points along the same way
options.misconception: keeps the direction while pretending to reverse

questions.explanation: Reversing the parameter reverses the derivative of the position vector, so the unit tangent changes sign and points the other way. The curve and its speed are unchanged.
questions.hint: Differentiate the reversed parameter and compare.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: assess a parallelism claim from the normals
questions.stem: Sheet 4150 reports that two planes with normals (1,2,0) and (2,4,0) were called parallel without checking, and asks for the assessment.

options.text: The claim is wrong, because parallel planes must have equal normal vectors
options.misconception: requires equal normals instead of parallel ones

options.text: The claim is right, because one normal is twice the other
The claim is wrong, because the constants on the right are not compared
options.misconception: requires a constant comparison that parallelism does not use

options.text: The claim is wrong, because the two planes meet along a common line
options.misconception: claims an intersection that parallel normals rule out

questions.explanation: Parallel planes have parallel normals, and (2,4,0) is exactly twice (1,2,0), so the direction test passes. The constants may still differ, and that difference only sets the separation.
questions.hint: One normal is a scalar multiple of the other.

questions.learningObjective: compute a distance from a point to a plane
questions.stem: Sheet 4151 asks for the distance from the point (1,0,1) to the plane 2x minus 3y plus z equals 8.
questions.explanation: The plane expression at the point is 2 plus 1 minus 8, which is minus 5 in absolute value, and the normal has length the root of 14, giving 1.3363.
questions.hint: Take the absolute value, then divide by the normal length.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Distance between parallel planes
questions.learningObjective: compute the gap shown in a diagram
questions.stem: Sheet 4152 shows two parallel contour surfaces labelled 2x plus y equals 4 and 2x plus y equals 9, and asks for the gap.

options.text: The gap is 5, the difference of the two constants
options.misconception: ignores the normal length when measuring the separation

options.text: The gap is 5 times the root of 5, the difference times the normal length
options.misconception: multiplies by the normal length instead of dividing

options.text: The gap is 5 over the root of 5, which is the root of 5
The gap is zero, since the two surfaces have the same normal
options.misconception: confuses parallel planes with coincident ones

questions.explanation: The separation is the constant difference, 5, divided by the length of the normal, the root of 5, giving the root of 5. Using the constants alone ignores the tilt of the surfaces.
questions.hint: Divide the constant difference by the normal length.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Magnitude of a vector in space
questions.learningObjective: predict how a length changes under scaling
questions.stem: Sheet 4153 asks how the length of a vector changes when its components are all scaled by the same factor.

options.text: It grows by that factor, since each component grew by it
options.misconception: treats the length as a sum of components

options.text: It grows by the square of the factor, since the components are squared
options.misconception: confuses the growth of the sum of squares with the length

options.text: It is unchanged, since the direction is what matters for a length
options.misconception: claims direction and length are the same thing

options.text: It grows by the same factor, since lengths scale with the vector

questions.explanation: Scaling a vector by a factor scales its length by that factor, because the square root of the scaled sum of squares pulls the factor back out. The direction of the vector is unchanged by the scaling.
questions.hint: The root of the scaled sum of squares brings the factor out.

questions.explanation: The curve has derivative (1,2,6) at that point, whose length is the root of 41, so the first component of the unit tangent is about 0.1562.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Line as the intersection of two planes
questions.learningObjective: state the condition for two planes to meet in a line
questions.stem: Sheet 4155 asks what must be true of the normals of two planes that meet in a line.

options.text: They must not be parallel, since parallel planes never meet in a line
They must be equal, since meeting planes share every direction
options.misconception: requires equal normals for a shared edge

options.text: They must be perpendicular, since a line needs two right angles
options.misconception: invents a right angle between the two planes

options.text: They must have unit length, since the shared line needs a unit normal
options.misconception: confuses the length of a normal with that of a unit vector

questions.explanation: Two planes meet in a line exactly when their normals are not parallel, so the cross product of the normals gives the direction of the line. Equal or perpendicular normals are not required.
questions.hint: Parallel normals give no shared line at all.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Unit vectors along a direction
questions.learningObjective: state what a unit vector cannot reveal
questions.stem: Sheet 4156 asks what a unit vector cannot tell you about the direction it points along.

options.text: It cannot tell you the heading, since the entries are just fractions
options.misconception: denies the obvious purpose of a unit vector

options.text: It cannot tell you the distance along that direction, since its length is one
It cannot tell you the line of travel, since a vector has no position
options.misconception: denies that a direction vector still gives a heading

options.text: It cannot tell you the heading of the line, since a heading needs two points
options.misconception: claims a direction vector fails to record a heading

questions.explanation: A unit vector records the heading, with its length fixed at one, so it says nothing about how far along that direction a point lies. The missing information is the distance or the position.
questions.hint: A unit vector fixes the heading and nothing else.

questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of a very large intercept
questions.stem: Sheet 4158 asks what happens to the intercept form when one of the cut distances becomes very large.

options.text: The term with that denominator becomes negligible, leaving the other two cuts
The whole equation becomes invalid, because the intercept is not finite

options.misconception: invents a compensation between the three denominators

options.text: All three terms shrink together, because the intercepts are related
options.misconception: claims the intercepts are tied to one another

options.misconception: invents a doubling effect from a sign change
